logline: A brilliant but rule-breaking philosophy teacher arrives at a Barcelona high school and forces his students - and himself - to apply Nietzsche, Hume, and Schopenhauer to the actual chaos of adolescent life.

renewal.note: Three-season run on TV3 concluded January 2018. A Netflix spinoff, Merlí: Sapere Aude, followed in December 2019 focusing on character Pol Rubau at university.

bollymeter.basis: 89% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Season 1 premiere drew 566,000 viewers - a 17.7% share on TV3, exceptional for a regional Catalan broadcast.

seasons.review_body: Merlí debuted on TV3 in September 2015 and became the most-watched drama in the channel's recent history. The premise - a charismatic, unorthodox philosophy teacher who applies the actual ideas of Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Hume to his students' real problems - was deceptively simple but executed with uncommon intelligence. Season 1 earned 566,000 viewers at a 17.7% audience share for its premiere. The show made Francesc Orella a breakout figure in Spanish television and Carlos Cuevas (as student Pol) a star. International critics who discovered it on Netflix responded to its refusal to infantilise its teenage characters.

episode_reviews.title: Els peripatètics
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes Merlí as a teacher who will use philosophy not as decoration but as genuine problem-solving tools - and the students who resist this most become the most compelling characters.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Merlí's first classroom session applying Aristotle's Peripatetics to a class of sceptical teenagers - the moment the show reveals its actual ambition.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 peaked at a 22.5% audience share on TV3 - higher than Season 1, indicating a show that grew its audience through word of mouth.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 arrived in September 2016 and increased its TV3 viewership share to a peak of 22.5%. The show deepened its exploration of student sexuality and family dysfunction while expanding the philosophical framework into more ambitious territory. The Pol and Bruno relationship became a central narrative axis, and the show's treatment of queer coming-of-age drew particular attention from international audiences discovering it via Netflix. Season 2 stands out as the point where the ensemble's dynamics reached full maturity and the philosophical conceits stopped feeling like a gimmick.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 sharpens everything Season 1 introduced, with student arcs that now carry real emotional weight from established context.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 finale drew 693,000 viewers at 23.6% audience share on TV3 - the highest single episode of the entire run, suggesting a show that maintained and grew its audience to the end.

seasons.review_body: The final season, which ran from September 2017 to January 2018, delivered the show's highest single-episode audience - the series finale drew 693,000 viewers at a 23.6% share on TV3. Season 3 introduced 14 episodes (one more than prior seasons) and accelerated several character trajectories toward resolution. The show's willingness to let Merlí himself be morally complicated - charming, brilliant, but not always good - paid off in the final run. The National Award for Television in 2019 for the series confirmed its standing as one of the most significant Catalan-language productions of the decade.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 goes longer and widens the character scope, trading some of Season 2's intimacy for a more operatic conclusion.

episode_reviews.title: Merlí
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale drew the show's highest ever audience - 693,000 viewers - and closes the Merlí chapter with an emotional honesty that rewards three seasons of investment.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Merlí's final scene with Pol - the teacher-student dynamic that powered the show reaching its natural, unsentimentalised conclusion.
